charts.annotation: Phosphates and Fertilizantes buy ammonia and sulfur as key raw materials; a spike here (e.g. FY2026) squeezes segment margin ahead of any selling-price pass-through.

segmentVolume.title: Segment sales volume
segmentVolume.content:
Tonnes sold in the period for each of Mosaic's three segments: Potash (mainly muriate of potash, MOP), Phosphates (mainly DAP/MAP) and Mosaic Fertilizantes, the Brazilian distribution business that blends Mosaic-produced and third-party-purchased product.

For Mosaic: volume moves with planting-season demand and Mosaic's own operating rates, while price moves with the global nutrient cycle -- the two drivers rarely point the same way in the same quarter.

What to watch:

  • Potash and Phosphates volume falling even as Fertilizantes (a lower-margin reseller of purchased product) grows
  • Volume dips that coincide with planned plant turnarounds versus genuine demand weakness

segmentAsp.title: Average selling price by product
segmentAsp.content:
Average realized price per tonne for Mosaic's headline products: MOP (potash), DAP (phosphate) and Brazil MAP (Fertilizantes). These track global benchmark fertilizer prices, not Mosaic's cost base.

For Mosaic: all three are commodity prices Mosaic does not set -- they are driven by global supply (China/Russia/Belarus export policy, new phosphate/potash capacity) and crop economics, so margin is mostly won or lost on cost control, not pricing power.

What to watch:

  • ASP direction versus the input-cost chart -- rising ASP with flat or falling input costs is the margin-expansion case
  • Divergence between MOP and DAP/MAP (potash and phosphate cycles don't always move together)

inputCosts.title: Ammonia and sulfur input costs
inputCosts.content:
Per-tonne cost of the two key raw materials Phosphates and Fertilizantes buy: ammonia (a nitrogen source used in DAP/MAP production) and sulfur (used to make the sulfuric acid that digests phosphate rock). Potash has no equivalent line -- it doesn't consume either input at scale.

For Mosaic: both are themselves volatile commodities set by global energy and sulfur markets, largely outside Mosaic's control; FY2026 saw both roughly double from FY2024-25 levels, well ahead of any DAP/MAP price pass-through, which is the direct cause of the FY2026 Phosphates margin compression visible in the EBITDA chart.

What to watch:

  • Input cost spikes that outrun the ASP chart -- the gap is margin given up this quarter
  • Blended rock cost (not charted here) as the third phosphate input, alongside ammonia and sulfur

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For The Mosaic Company: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For The Mosaic Company: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For The Mosaic Company: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For The Mosaic Company: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For The Mosaic Company: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For The Mosaic Company: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For The Mosaic Company: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For The Mosaic Company: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Mosaic: revenue is price times volume across three segments with different cycles (potash, phosphate, Brazil distribution) -- the Segment Operations charts below break it into those two drivers.

What to watch:

  • Whether a revenue move came from price (see Average Selling Price) or volume (see Segment Sales Volume)
  • Interim rows show planting-season seasonality, strongest in Q1-Q2

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For The Mosaic Company: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
